run.question: My AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 has high latency issues. Investigate why.

report.summary: The subject names an AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' in us-east-1, but this Run has no AWS/CloudWatch data source and no AWS CLI tool: only Kubernetes, Prometheus and Jaeger are available, so Lambda Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions and Lambda logs could not be queried. I fetched runbook 'lambda-performance-troubleshooting' and attempted its steps; all five (Duration statistics, log-pattern filter, InitDuration cold starts, ConcurrentExecutions, Logs Insights memory) require CloudWatch/`aws` CLI, which this Run does not have, so none could be carried out. I substituted the analog entity that does exist in the target, the Kubernetes Deployment/Service 'payment' in namespace otel-demo, which is a different entity from the named Lambda: it is 1/1 ready, its pod payment-6f7bc865d6-wwqnm is Running, ready, restart count 0 with no previous container instance, and its sampled application log shows 'Charge request received' followed about 1 ms later by 'Transaction complete' with no error-level lines in the newest 80 of 188 lines. The in-cluster fault flags 'paymentFailure' and 'paymentUnreachable' in flagd-config are both defaultVariant 'off'. Latency itself could not be measured for any service: every Prometheus call and every Jaeger call returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE, so there is no duration, error-rate or span evidence and no baseline for a trend. No Kubernetes events fell in the window (query returned no_data). Net: the Lambda's high latency cannot be confirmed, characterised or attributed here; the latency question is unresolved rather than shown absent or healthy.

claims.text: The only workload named 'payment' in this target is the Kubernetes Deployment 'payment' in namespace otel-demo, reporting 1 ready of 1 replicas with image ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.0.2-payment on container port 8080; it is a Kubernetes workload, not the AWS Lambda function 'payment-processor' the subject names.
A single Service named 'payment' exists in namespace otel-demo, and no other Service name or label matching 'payment' was returned among the 29 services read.
No pod in the cluster has a name matching 'payment-processor' or 'lambda' (case-insensitive) among the 32 pods read, so the Lambda execution environment is not visible in this Kubernetes target.

Pod payment-6f7bc865d6-wwqnm (owner ReplicaSet payment-6f7bc865d6, node opspilot-m1-control-plane) is Running and ready with restartCount 0 and an empty lastState; there is no previous container instance to read, so no crash or restart evidence exists for it.

The payment container's sampled application log (newest 80 of 188 lines, 2026-11-23T15:59:58Z to 16:24:26Z) contains only level=info entries: each 'Charge request received.' is followed within roughly 1 ms by 'Transaction complete.' with a transactionId; no error-, warn-, timeout- or failure-level line appears in the shown lines.

The in-cluster fault-injection flags affecting payment — 'paymentFailure' ("Fail payment service charge requests n%") and 'paymentUnreachable' ("Payment service is unavailable") — are both state ENABLED with defaultVariant 'off' in ConfigMap flagd-config, so no payment failure or unreachability fault was switched on in this cluster when the setting was read.

The reported Lambda latency cannot be attributed from this target: if it is real, the signal would have to come from Lambda Duration/InitDuration (cold starts) or ConcurrentExecutions in CloudWatch plus Lambda log REPORT/maxMemoryUsed lines, none of which any available source exposes in this Run; this is a hypothesis about where the signal lives, not an observed cause.

Connect a CloudWatch (metrics and logs) data source for us-east-1 or provide an AWS CLI-capable tool, then run the 'lambda-performance-troubleshooting' queries against function 'payment-processor': Duration Average/Maximum per 300s, an [ERROR]/[WARN]/timeout log filter, InitDuration Average/Count, ConcurrentExecutions Maximum per 60s, and a Logs Insights max(@maxMemoryUsed) vs avg(@memorySize) query.

gaps: No AWS Lambda or CloudWatch data source and no AWS CLI tool are configured in this Run (available sources are jaeger, knowledge, kubernetes, prometheus), so Duration, InitDuration, ConcurrentExecutions, throttles and Lambda log groups for 'payment-processor' in us-east-1 were not observable; the runbook's steps 1-5 were not carried out.

All Prometheus calls (get_metric_names, get_label_values, execute_prometheus_instant_query, metrics_range_query, get_prometheus_target, list_prometheus_rules) and both Jaeger calls (traces_list_services, traces_search for service 'payment') returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE between 2026-11-23T16:26:11Z and 16:26:26Z, so no latency, error-rate or span evidence was available and no latency trend or baseline comparison was possible.

The Kubernetes events query for the authorized window returned status no_data (total_items_processed 0), so in-cluster change, create and restart history for the payment workload during the window is unknown, not absent.

The payment log view is marked incomplete: 80 newest of 188 matching lines were shown (108 omitted) covering only 15:59:58Z-16:26:17Z, so error lines earlier in the window are unknown; log line deltas are not span latency.
Whether the named Lambda function 'payment-processor' exists or is healthy is unknown; the cluster's 'payment' Deployment/Service is a different entity and its state says nothing about the Lambda.
next_steps: Enable a CloudWatch (metrics and logs) integration for us-east-1 and re-run the lambda-performance-troubleshooting queries for function 'payment-processor', comparing Duration p50/p95/max against a pre-incident baseline.
Check Lambda InitDuration and cold-start counts for 'payment-processor' before and after the first slow period, since cold starts are a distinct latency mechanism from steady-state Duration.

Obtain working Prometheus and Jaeger access for target m0-otel-20260909 (all calls returned SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE) so the in-cluster payment service durations and error spans can be checked against a comparable baseline.

content.name: lambda-performance-troubleshooting
content.content:
# AWS Lambda High Latency Troubleshooting

## Overview
This runbook helps diagnose and resolve AWS Lambda function performance issues including high latency, timeouts, and cold starts.

## Steps

### Step 1: Query Performance Metrics
Use CloudWatch to check Lambda function latency over time:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name Duration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 2: Check Function Logs
Look for errors or slow operations in CloudWatch Logs:
```bash
aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --filter-pattern "[ERROR] OR [WARN] OR timeout" --limit 100
```

### Step 3: Analyze Cold Start Patterns
Query CloudWatch for cold start frequency:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name InitDuration --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Average,Count --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 300
```

### Step 4: Check Concurrent Executions
Verify Lambda isn't hitting concurrency limits:
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace <lambda-namespace> \
  --metric-name ConcurrentExecutions --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=<function-name> \
  --statistics Maximum --start-time <start-time> \
  --end-time <end-time> --period 60
```

### Step 5: Review Memory Utilization
Check if function needs more memory allocation:
```bash
aws logs insights start-query --log-group-name <lambda-log-group>/<function-name> \
  --start-time <epoch-start> --end-time <epoch-end> \
  --query-string "fields @timestamp, @message | filter @type = 'REPORT' | stats max(@maxMemoryUsed), avg(@memorySize)"
```
